summary: Describes the OSPFv2 extensions required for Segment Routing. OSPF is used to advertise the segments that nodes can use to build end-to-end paths as sequences of subpaths within the network.

eli5.summary: Routers already share maps with each other. This adds the extra signposts needed to build paths from pieces, using the OSPF map-sharing protocol for IPv4.

questions: what is a prefix sid in ospf
subtitle: How OSPFv2 routers advertise the labels and identifiers that let a path be built from segments.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing encodes an end-to-end path as a list of segments, but routers need a way to tell each other which segment identifiers (SIDs) they own and which label ranges they use.
tldr.mechanism: OSPFv2 carries this in new TLVs and sub-TLVs inside Opaque LSAs: router capabilities (algorithms, label ranges) in the Router Information LSA, and Prefix-SIDs and Adjacency SIDs in the Extended Prefix and Extended Link LSAs.
tldr.outcome: With these extensions OSPFv2 can program the MPLS data plane as well as the IP data plane, so SR paths need no LDP or RSVP-TE signaling. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 8665 is a Proposed Standard, published in December 2019, and has not been obsoleted or updated. The matching IS-IS encodings are in RFC 8667, and OSPFv3 is covered by RFC 8666.

sections.title: Segments Carried by OSPFv2
sections.content:
Segment Routing (SR) describes an end-to-end path inside an IGP network as a sequence of segments, which are topological subpaths. The link-state protocols (IS-IS and OSPF) advertise those segments.

A prefix segment is an ECMP-aware shortest path to a prefix or a node, and is typically multi-hop. An adjacency segment is a hop over one specific adjacency between two nodes, and is usually a one-hop path.

SR can run over IPv6 or MPLS data planes. This RFC covers only OSPFv2, which supports just the IPv4 address family, so the IPv6 data plane is out of scope. With MPLS, SR paths need no LDP or RSVP-TE signaling, though SR can interoperate with LSPs set up by them. The architecture itself is in RFC 8402.
sections.eli5: Instead of one long set of directions, a trip is split into short pieces. Some pieces are long roads to a place and some are just one step across a bridge. OSPF shares the names of all those pieces.

sections.title: Identifiers and the SID/Label Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The SID types covered are Prefix-SID, Adjacency SID, LAN Adjacency SID and Binding SID. They are advertised with the Extended Prefix and Extended Link Opaque LSAs from RFC 7684.

The SID/Label Sub-TLV (Type 1) is the common building block that appears inside many other TLVs. Its Length is 3 or 4 octets. If the length is 3, the 20 rightmost bits are a label. If it is 4, the value is a 32-bit SID.
sections.eli5: A SID is a name tag. Sometimes the tag is a short ticket number and sometimes it is a longer one, so the tag says which size it is.

sections.title: Router Capabilities and Label Ranges
sections.content:
Each SR router advertises its capabilities in the Router Information (RI) Opaque LSA from RFC 7770. These TLVs are shared with OSPFv3 (RFC 8666).

  • SR-Algorithm TLV (Type 8): lists the algorithms the router uses. Algorithm 0 is normal metric-based SPF, which a node may override by local policy. Algorithm 1 is Strict SPF, where local policy MUST NOT alter the path. If the TLV is sent, Algorithm 0 MUST be included. A node that does not advertise it is not SR capable. Area-scoped flooding is REQUIRED.
  • SID/Label Range TLV (Type 9): a 3-octet Range Size (greater than 0) plus a SID/Label Sub-TLV giving the first label. Several ranges can be sent, and receivers MUST use the advertised order when turning an index into a label. Ranges MUST NOT overlap.
  • SR Local Block TLV (Type 14): the labels the node has reserved for local SIDs, such as Adjacency SIDs. It has the same layout as the range TLV.
  • SRMS Preference TLV (Type 15): a one-octet preference from 0 to 255 for a node acting as an SR Mapping Server. AS-scoped flooding SHOULD be used because mapping servers can be in a different area from their consumers.

If a router sends a Prefix-SID with an algorithm that its originator has not advertised in the SR-Algorithm TLV, receivers MUST ignore that Prefix-SID.
sections.eli5: Before a router hands out name tags it announces which kinds of route-finding it knows and which block of numbers it will use for its tags, so everyone can read them correctly.

sections.title: Prefix-SID and the Extended Prefix Range TLV
sections.content:
The Prefix-SID Sub-TLV (Type 2) attaches a SID to a prefix. Its fields are Flags, Reserved, MT-ID, Algorithm and the SID/Index/Label. The Length is 7 or 8 octets depending on the V-Flag.

  • NP: no penultimate hop popping. If set, the penultimate hop MUST NOT pop the Prefix-SID.
  • M: the SID came from an SR Mapping Server.
  • E: Explicit Null. Upstream neighbors replace the SID with the Explicit NULL label (0 for IPv4).
  • V and L: whether the field is an absolute value or an index, and whether it is local or global.

Only two V/L settings are valid. With both 0, the field is a 4-octet index into the SID/Label space the router advertised. With both 1, it is a 3-octet local label using the 20 rightmost bits. Any other combination MUST be ignored. If a router advertises several Prefix-SIDs for the same prefix, topology and algorithm, all are ignored.

With NP clear, upstream neighbors pop the SID. With NP set and E clear, they keep it on top of the stack, which helps an ABR or ASBR stitch into a continuing LSP. With both set, they swap it for Explicit NULL.

The OSPF Extended Prefix Range TLV (Type 2) advertises SIDs for a whole contiguous range of prefixes in one go, mainly for SR Mapping Servers. It holds a Prefix Length, an AF (0 for IPv4 unicast), a Range Size, an IA (inter-area) flag and the address prefix. For example, four loopbacks from 192.0.2.1/32 with indexes 1 to 4 become one TLV with prefix 192.0.2.1, length 32, Range Size 4 and index 1.
sections.eli5: A Prefix-SID is a name tag stuck on a place. The tag has little switches that say things like 'take this tag off one step early' or 'keep it on until the end'. One list can name a whole row of houses at once.

sections.title: Adjacency SIDs
sections.content:
An Adj-SID names a router adjacency. The Adj-SID Sub-TLV (Type 2) sits inside the Extended Link TLV and may appear several times. Its flags are B (eligible for fast-reroute protection), V, L, G (the SID refers to a group of adjacencies) and P (persistent across restart or interface flap). It also carries a one-octet Weight for load balancing, defined in RFC 8402.

A router MAY allocate an Adj-SID for each adjacency, more than one for the same adjacency, or the same one for different adjacencies. If the P-Flag is set, the Adj-SID MUST be persistent.

On broadcast, NBMA or hybrid networks, routers only advertise their adjacency to the Designated Router, so the LAN Adj-SID Sub-TLV (Type 3) additionally carries the Neighbor ID, the Router ID of the non-DR neighbor it applies to.

On point-to-point links an Adj-SID MAY be advertised for a neighbor in state 2-Way or higher, and MUST be withdrawn if the adjacency drops below 2-Way.
sections.eli5: An Adj-SID is a tag for one single step between two neighbors, like 'cross this bridge'. Some tags can be kept for good, even if the bridge is closed for a while.

sections.title: Intra-area, Inter-area and External Prefixes
sections.content:
Within an area, a router MAY advertise Prefix-SIDs for any prefix it advertises, such as a loopback. A Mapping Server can advertise Prefix-SIDs for remote prefixes and MUST use the Extended Prefix Range TLV. When several mapping servers cover the same prefix, they MUST advertise the same Prefix-SID.

To work across areas, OSPFv2 MUST propagate Prefix-SID information. When an ABR originates a Type-3 Summary LSA, it also originates an area-scoped Extended Prefix Opaque LSA with route type inter-area. It copies the Prefix-SID from the router on its best path, or from any other router if that one advertised none. ABRs set the IA-Flag on propagated range TLVs and only forward the best one.

For external prefixes, an SR-capable ASBR SHOULD also originate an AS-scoped Extended Prefix Opaque LSA with route type external next to its Type-5 LSA. An NSSA ABR that translates Type-7 into Type-5 SHOULD advertise the Prefix-SID too. For prefixes an ABR or ASBR re-advertises, NP MUST be set and E MUST be clear unless the prefix is directly attached.
sections.eli5: When a message crosses from one neighborhood to another, the border guard copies the name tags across so the tags still make sense on the other side.

sections.title: Errors, IANA and Security
sections.content:
If the length of any new TLV or sub-TLV is invalid, the whole LSA is considered malformed and MUST be ignored, with a rate-limited error log. IANA assigned the TLV types above and created the IGP Algorithm Type registry (values 0 to 255, Standards Action), with 0 and 1 as the initial entries.

OSPFv2 now programs the MPLS data plane in addition to the IP data plane, which previously needed LDP or another label distribution mechanism. Attacks on the IP control plane can be carried out on the MPLS control plane too, and may be harder to detect and isolate. The existing security extensions of RFC 2328 and RFC 7684 apply, and in deployments where attackers may reach the network, stronger authentication such as that of RFC 7474 SHOULD be used. Implementations MUST ensure malformed TLVs cannot crash the OSPFv2 router.
sections.eli5: If a name tag is the wrong size, the router throws away that whole note and writes it down. Because these tags now steer real traffic, the routers should check who is sending them.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: 7 or 8 octets, depending on the V-Flag.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: NP, M, E, V and L flags.

fields.name: Algorithm
fields.desc: Algorithm the Prefix-SID is associated with.

fields.name: SID/Index/Label
fields.desc: Index, or local label, depending on the V and L flags.
